opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that plugins assume you already know where the seams are. When you design a plugin system, you're making a bet up front about which parts of the system will need to change and which parts are stable. That works well when the humans building the core have a good model of what users will want. But once you have an agent as a real collaborator on the codebase, that bet starts to look pretty conservative.

With a plugin model like OpenClaw's, the agent can only extend the system along the axes we anticipated. If the right fix is to restructure how scheduling works, or change how state flows between components, a plugin can't do that. You end up with workarounds layered on workarounds, because the agent is trying to express an architectural change through an interface that was never meant to carry it.

What we wanted to explore with Exo is: what if the architecture itself is the thing the agent is allowed to reason about and modify? Not recklessly, but with the same kind of guardrails you'd put around a senior engineer. You need good tests, clear invariants, the ability to roll back, and some way of evaluating whether a change actually made things better. If you have those, then letting the agent touch the core stops being scary and starts being the interesting part.

And I think there's a deeper point. A lot of the value in software comes from reshaping abstractions, not adding features at the edges. If agents are only ever allowed to add features at the edges, we're capping them at the least interesting kind of work. So for us it's partly a practical choice and partly a research question: how much of the system can you hand over, and what infrastructure do you need to make that safe?

I'll be honest, it's not free. You give up some predictability, and debugging is harder when the shape of the system can shift underneath you. But I'd rather confront those problems directly than pretend the plugin boundary is where the hard problems stop.

r001.rationale: It says plugin systems depend on humans anticipating which parts will change, limiting agents to those predetermined extension points.

r002.rationale: It says Exo should let the agent reason about and modify the architecture itself.

r003.rationale: It argues that agents should be able to reshape architecture, but does not cite increasing model capability as a reason to avoid human-prescribed architectures.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the plugin model is really seductive because it feels safe. You give the agent a stable core, you expose a bunch of hooks, and you let it bolt on tools or skills at the edges. That's what OpenClaw does, and honestly for a lot of use cases that's totally fine. But I think it fundamentally caps what the thing can become, and the reason is that the core is where all the interesting decisions live.

Think about what actually determines whether an agent is good. It's not really which tools it has access to. It's how it decides when to call them, how it manages its own context window, how it structures memory, how it decomposes a task, when it asks for help versus pushes forward. Those are architectural choices. And in a plugin world, the humans made all of those choices once, up front, and froze them. The agent is just furnishing a house someone else designed.

What we noticed building Exo is that the agent is often the one with the best information about where its own architecture is failing. It's the one hitting the context limit at the wrong moment. It's the one realizing its retrieval strategy keeps surfacing stale stuff. If the only lever it has is "add another plugin," it ends up with this sprawling accumulation of patches around a core it can't touch. You've all seen codebases like that. It's the same pathology, just happening to the agent itself.

So the bet with Exo is: treat the whole thing as mutable. The orchestration loop, the memory layer, the way it represents its own goals. The agent can propose changes, test them against its own evaluation harness, and adopt them if they're better. Yes, that sounds terrifying, and I want to be honest that it is harder to reason about. But we think the safety story is actually stronger when the self-modification is explicit and observable, with versioning and rollback and a real eval gate, versus the implicit version where a plugin quietly changes behavior in ways nobody designed for.

The analogy I keep coming back to is the difference between a config file and a compiler. Plugins are config. You can get a long way with config. But at some point, if you want the system to genuinely improve at the thing it's for, you have to let it touch the code.

r001.rationale: The response says humans choose the architecture up front and freeze it, while OpenClaw plugins add tools or skills at the edges.

r002.rationale: It proposes treating the whole system as mutable, including the orchestration loop and memory layer, so the agent can propose and adopt changes.

r003.rationale: The response argues that agents can identify their own architectural failures, but does not connect avoiding human-prescribed architectures to increasing model capability.

astra-6.text:
I think plugins assume you already know what the architecture should be—that you’ve picked the right abstractions, and the agent just needs more capabilities within them. But sometimes the thing limiting the agent is the structure itself: how it manages state, how it schedules work, or how different parts communicate. Adding another tool doesn’t necessarily fix that.

The idea with Exo is to let the agent question those assumptions. If it discovers a better way to organize itself for the task, it should be able to make that change, test it, and roll it back if it doesn’t work. That doesn’t mean rewriting everything all the time. Plugins can still be useful. I just don’t think they should define the boundary of what the agent is allowed to improve.

r001.rationale: The response says plugins assume someone has already chosen the right abstractions, making plugin customization depend on prior human architectural choices.

r002.rationale: It argues that Exo should let the agent change how it is organized, including its state management, scheduling, and communication.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention increasing model capability as a reason to avoid human-prescribed architectures.

sol-6.1.text:
The reason to let an agent change its architecture is that plugins still leave a person deciding what’s fixed and what’s extensible. You can give the agent more tools, but if the bottleneck is how it plans, manages context, or coordinates work, another tool may not solve it.

I’d want the agent to be able to question those choices too. Could it replace its planning loop? Change how it stores state? Try a different way of splitting up a task? That opens up a much larger space of possible improvements.

But the ability to rewrite itself isn’t evidence that the rewrite is better. You need a way to test the change, compare it with the existing system, and roll it back. The interesting part is closing that loop: letting the agent propose architectural changes and making it demonstrate that they help.

r001.rationale: It says plugins leave a person deciding what is fixed and extensible.

r002.rationale: It supports letting the agent change its architecture, with examples such as replacing its planning loop and changing how it stores state.

r003.rationale: It does not cite increasing model capability as a reason to avoid human-prescribed architectures.
